clue.text: Oriental responsible, perhaps, for part of the smokescreen in Drood

definitions.text: Oriental responsible, perhaps, for part of the smokescreen in Drood

parts.words: Oriental responsible, perhaps, for part of the smokescreen in Drood
parts.note: Dickens's unfinished Edwin Drood opens in a London opium den, where a Chinese man smokes alongside the old woman; the 'smokescreen' is the opium fug

explanation.surface: A literary query about who made the smoke in a Dickens mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Mystery of Edwin Drood the opium den has a rival keeper called by this name; 'smokescreen' is both the opium smoke and the plot's concealment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the name the old opium woman gives her Chinese rival proprietor in Dickens's novel.

clue.text: Late Powellian who gave ear on our behalf

definitions.text: who gave ear on our behalf

explanation.surface: A character from a novelist's later work who once listened for us.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Jenkins narrates Anthony Powell's twelve-volume A Dance to the Music of Time; Captain Robert Jenkins lost an ear to the Spanish, sparking the 1739 War of Jenkins' Ear on Britain's behalf.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrator of Powell's later sequence shares a surname with the sea captain whose severed ear began an Anglo-Spanish war.

clue.text: Flower of crime writer's creation

explanation.surface: A bloom created by a detective novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: A campion is a pink or white wild flower; Albert Campion is the gentleman sleuth invented by Margery Allingham.

clue.text: Focus on mouthpiece to reveal burglar's instrument

parts.note: a focus is the centre of attention
a bit is the metal mouthpiece of a horse's bridle

explanation.surface: Concentrating on a speaker's words exposes a thief's tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mouthpiece' suggests a spokesman or a telephone part, but it is the bit in a horse's mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: A centre bit is a drill bit with a central point, once a housebreaker's standard tool for boring through doors.

clue.text: People discovered in Spain (Castile)

indicators.note: something discovered in these words is found sitting within them, so the letters run across the words in brackets

explanation.surface: A nation found living in a region of Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas were the native Andean people whose empire Spain conquered.

clue.text: Sailors deceived reportedly run away

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said aloud, so the letters for these words are only heard

parts.note: ABS are able seamen, sailors, and conned means deceived

explanation.surface: Seamen tricked, so the story goes, and fled.
explanation.definitionFit: To abscond is to flee secretly, especially to escape justice.

clue.text: She waits, like Mrs Masham

explanation.surface: A woman who attends, as a famous courtier did.
explanation.walkthrough: Abigail Masham was Queen Anne's bedchamber woman and favourite; the name also became a general word for a lady's maid after a waiting-woman in a 17th-century play.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is an old word for a lady's maid and was also the first name of Queen Anne's favourite, Lady Masham.

clue.text: French literary high-flier

parts.note: high-flier is taken literally: a French writer who was also a pilot, author of The Little Prince

explanation.surface: A successful French author.
explanation.definitionFit: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry was an aviator as well as the author of The Little Prince and Night Flight.

clue.text: Scipio and Monty made such a name for themselves

definitions.text: Scipio and Monty made such a name for themselves

parts.words: Scipio and Monty made such a name for themselves
parts.note: Scipio earned Africanus and Montgomery 'of Alamein' from their victories, an extra name won by deeds

explanation.surface: Two generals became famous through their exploits.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnomen is a fourth Roman name added for some achievement, like Africanus.

clue.text: I shelter in fortress in old Spain

indicators.note: to shelter in somewhere is to be enclosed by it, so the letter goes inside the word for the fortress

parts.note: a castle is a fortress

explanation.surface: Someone takes refuge in a stronghold in historic Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Castile was a medieval kingdom at the heart of what became Spain.

clue.text: What they all did in 1918 for Sassoon

definitions.text: What they all did in 1918 for Sassoon

parts.words: What they all did in 1918 for Sassoon
parts.note: Siegfried Sassoon's poem celebrating the Armistice is titled with the action of everybody bursting into song

explanation.surface: A question about collective behaviour at the end of the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassoon's 1919 poem about the Armistice opens with the line that gives it its title.

clue.text: More uproarious ironies, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the word ironies is only a possible arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: Ironic remarks may make things livelier.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisier is the comparative of noisy, and uproarious means very loud.

clue.text: Boards hold alternative hoard

indicators.note: the boards hold another word, so it is placed inside them

parts.note: the boards is the theatre stage
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Theatres keep another option in reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: Storage is a place where things are kept stockpiled.

clue.text: Needs only collected edition including Western writer

indicators.note: the words Needs only are including the writer, so his name sits across them

explanation.surface: Only a complete edition will do for a cowboy novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collected edition' is surface padding; the name runs across 'Needs only'.
explanation.definitionFit: J. T. Edson was a prolific British author of cowboy novels.

clue.text: He illustrated one of Aubrey's lives

definitions.text: He illustrated one of Aubrey's lives

parts.words: He illustrated one of Aubrey's lives
parts.note: Aubrey suggests John Aubrey's Brief Lives, but this Aubrey is the artist, and the illustrator is one of his own lives

explanation.surface: An artist who drew pictures for John Aubrey's biographies.
explanation.walkthrough: John Aubrey wrote Brief Lives, so the clue seems to want an illustrator of that book; Aubrey is instead the illustrator's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Aubrey Beardsley was the Victorian black-and-white illustrator of Wilde's Salome.

clue.text: State and nation differently, a little faster

indicators.note: the words placed differently are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A country's politics shift slightly more quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' is a link inviting the solver to state the words rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Andantino is a musical tempo marking slightly quicker than andante.

clue.text: Peace-keepers strangely undated, and not afraid

parts.note: the UN, United Nations, sends peace-keeping forces

indicators.note: strangely signals the letters of undated are set out in an odd order

explanation.surface: United Nations troops oddly without a date yet still fearless.
explanation.definitionFit: Undaunted means not discouraged or intimidated by danger.

clue.text: Clotho's life source from hell river

parts.note: Dis is the Roman underworld
the Taff is a river in South Wales flowing through Cardiff

explanation.surface: A Fate's thread comes from an underworld river.
explanation.walkthrough: Clotho is the Fate who spins the thread of life; 'hell river' suggests the Styx but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A distaff is the staff holding wool for spinning, Clotho's tool for the thread of each life.

clue.text: Expedition revealing old city knowledge, supported by church

indicators.note: in a down entry, supported by means the church comes underneath, so after

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Sumerian city
gen is slang for information
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: An archaeological journey uncovering an ancient city, backed by the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' looks like a journey but means haste; the answer is an old word for urgency.
explanation.definitionFit: Expedition can mean speed or promptness, and urgence is an archaic form of urgency.

clue.text: Its young distinguished from Hawk by Hamlet

definitions.text: Its young distinguished from Hawk by Hamlet

parts.words: Its young distinguished from Hawk by Hamlet
parts.note: Hamlet says he knows a hawk from a handsaw, often explained as hernshaw, a young wading bird

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean prince tells a bird's chick from a raptor.
explanation.definitionFit: A hernshaw is a young heron, the wading bird Hamlet's handsaw is taken to mean.

clue.text: Namesake of Roman chap, friend of Pistol

parts.note: homo is the Latin word for a man
Nym is Pistol's crony in Shakespeare's Henry V and The Merry Wives of Windsor

explanation.surface: A Roman man shares a name with a Shakespearean soldier's comrade.
explanation.definitionFit: A word with the same form as another is its namesake in the dictionary sense.

clue.text: "Grishkin is nice: her — eye / Is underlined for emphasis" (T. S. Eliot)

definitions.text: "Grishkin is nice: her — eye / Is underlined for emphasis" (T. S. Eliot)

parts.words: "Grishkin is nice: her — eye / Is underlined for emphasis" (T. S. Eliot)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Eliot's Whispers of Immortality, where the missing word is the nationality of Grishkin's eye

explanation.surface: A quotation from Eliot with a word removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's line describes Grishkin's eye as from Russia, in Whispers of Immortality.

clue.text: Flag officers?

parts.note: read not as admirals but as both flags and junior officers, a word meaning each

explanation.surface: Senior naval commanders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag officers' are admirals, but the word wanted means both flags and junior officers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ensigns are banners, especially naval flags, and also the lowest commissioned officers.

clue.text: Rebellious Danes in the chair FROM THIS ISSUE, THE CROSSWORD WILL APPEAR WEEKLY

indicators.note: rebellious Danes refuse to keep in line, so their letters change order

explanation.surface: Unruly Scandinavians take the chair.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedan is a sedan chair, an enclosed seat carried on poles.

clue.text: Retribution seems in order

indicators.note: put in order, the letters of seems in are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: Punishment appears appropriate.
explanation.definitionFit: Nemesis is the Greek goddess of vengeance, and so deserved punishment.

clue.text: Pined in ruined deanery

indicators.note: a ruined building has its parts tumbled, so the letters of deanery fall into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone longed for something in a derelict dean's house.
explanation.definitionFit: To pine and to yearn both mean to long wistfully.

clue.text: Bush (not required where good wine available)

definitions.text: Bush (not required where good wine available)

parts.words: Bush (not required where good wine available)
parts.note: the proverb 'good wine needs no bush' refers to the ivy bush once hung outside taverns to advertise them

explanation.surface: A shrub is unnecessary where fine wine is sold.
explanation.walkthrough: A bush of ivy was the old sign of a tavern; the proverb says good wine sells without one.
explanation.definitionFit: The bush hung outside a tavern was its advertising board, the forerunner of the painted pub board.

clue.text: Early Powellian chaps (PM and followers)

parts.note: p.m. is the time after midday
men are followers, as of a leader

explanation.surface: A prime minister and his supporters appear in a novelist's first book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PM' looks like Prime Minister but means post meridiem; the answer is Anthony Powell's first novel (1931).
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Powell's debut novel names its idle young male characters.
